wording: A systematic review of quantitative studies (1872–2010) reports that religion/spirituality is related to better mental health on average, with some studies showing negative or mixed associations.
locator: 'related to better mental health (less depression, lower stress...)'; mixed/negative counts in subsections
counterevidence_limits: Single-author review; observational designs dominate; publication bias not assessed here.

wording: In the Nurses' Health Study (n = 74,534), attending religious services more than once per week vs never was associated with lower all-cause mortality (HR 0.67, 95% CI 0.62–0.71); authors note possible unmeasured and residual confounding.
counterevidence_limits: Women, mostly white US nurses; self-reported attendance.

wording: Many 'spirituality' measures are contaminated with mental-health and positive-character items, making some spirituality–health associations tautological.
counterevidence_limits: Critics replied in the same journal (comments listed in PubMed record); not read this pass.

wording: In the SEP's account, mystical experience is defined to exclude paranormal experiences such as visions or voices, and mysticism is best understood as practices, texts and traditions aimed at transformation, not only experiences.
counterevidence_limits: Definitions vary across scholars and traditions.

wording: For HR 0.67 the E-value is 2.35 (rare-outcome approximation) or 1.97 after common-outcome conversion (outcome risk 18%); CI-limit E-values 2.17 / 1.85.
counterevidence_limits: E-value is a bound, not evidence that confounding exists or not.

wording: The SIM-R4-C0 Monte Carlo check E2 FAILED because its confounder parameterisation did not implement the E-value's definition; no conclusion is drawn from it.
